summary.text: Positivity applied to \((N+4)!/6\) supplies a decomposition \((N+4)!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\), with \(6x-1\) Sophie Germain and \(6y-1,6y+1\) twin primes. If either family were bounded by \(N\), the relevant prime (\(6x-1\), or \(6y+1\) lying two above the bounded lower twin) would divide the factorial and hence the other summand; primality then forces it to be \(1\) or equal to that summand, contradicting positivity and their incompatible residues modulo \(6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }p+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set whose elements are the smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

Assume that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1,
\]
where \(a(n)\) counts the decompositions \(n=x+y\), with \(x,y>0\), for which
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. We prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

First, we record exactly what the positivity assumption supplies. For every integer \(n>1\), the number \(a(n)\) is a finite sum over the integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\). The summand belonging to \(x\) is \(1\) precisely when, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are prime, and otherwise that summand is \(0\). If the sum is positive, at least one summand is nonzero. Therefore, for every \(n>1\), there exist positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\tag{1}
\]
are all prime. Notice that \(12x-1=2(6x-1)+1\), so the first two primality conditions say that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Similarly,
\[
(6y-1)+2=6y+1,
\]
so the last two conditions say that \(6y-1\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair.

We next construct a decomposition adapted to an arbitrary bound \(N\). Let
\[
F=(N+4)!.
\]
Since \(4!=24\) divides \((N+4)!\), the number \(6\) divides \(F\). Write
\[
F=6n
\]
for an integer \(n\). Moreover, \(F\ge 4!=24\), so \(6n\ge24\) and hence \(n\ge4>1\). Applying the consequence of the positivity hypothesis just established, choose positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and all four numbers in (1) are prime. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
(6x-1)+(6y+1)
  &=6x+6y\\
  &=6(x+y)\\
  &=6n\\
  &=(N+4)!.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
Thus, for every \(N\), there are positive integers \(x,y\) satisfying (1) and (2).

We now prove that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes. Suppose, to the contrary, that \(S\) is finite. A finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound, so choose \(N\) such that every element of \(S\) is at most \(N\). Apply the preceding factorial construction for this \(N\), and set
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
By (1), both \(p\) and \(12x-1\) are prime. Since
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
we have \(p\in S\). Consequently,
\[
p\le N.
\tag{3}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, it is positive; together with (3), this gives
\[
1\le p\le N<N+4.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(N+4\) divides \((N+4)!\), because it occurs among the factors in that factorial. Hence
\[
p\mid (N+4)!.
\]
On the other hand, equation (2) says
\[
(N+4)!=p+q.
\]
Since \(p\mid p\) and \(p\mid p+q\), subtraction gives
\[
p\mid q.
\tag{4}
\]
But \(q=6y+1\) is prime by (1). The only positive divisors of a prime are \(1\) and the prime itself, so (4) implies either
\[
p=1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
p=q.
\]
Neither is possible. Since \(x\ge1\),
\[
p=6x-1\ge5,
\]
so \(p\ne1\). Also, \(p=6x-1\) is congruent to \(-1\pmod 6\), whereas \(q=6y+1\) is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\). Equality would therefore imply \(-1\equiv1\pmod6\), or equivalently that \(6\) divides \(2\), which is impossible. This contradiction proves that \(S\) is infinite.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs. Suppose instead that \(T\) is finite. Choose an integer \(N\) which bounds all of its elements. Again apply the factorial construction for this \(N\), and now put
\[
t=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1=t+2,
\qquad p=6x-1.
\]
The numbers \(t\) and \(q=t+2\) are both prime by (1), so \(t\in T\). By the choice of \(N\),
\[
t\le N.
\]
It follows that
\[
q=t+2\le N+2\le N+4.
\]
As \(q\) is positive, it is one of the positive integers not exceeding \(N+4\), and therefore
\[
q\mid (N+4)!.
\]
Using (2), this says that \(q\mid p+q\). Since also \(q\mid q\), subtraction yields
\[
q\mid p.
\tag{5}
\]
The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Thus (5) forces either
\[
q=1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
q=p.
\]
Again both alternatives are impossible. Since \(y\ge1\), we have \(q=6y+1\ge7\), so \(q\ne1\). And \(q\equiv1\pmod6\), while \(p\equiv-1\pmod6\), so they cannot be equal. This contradiction proves that \(T\) is infinite.

Therefore the assumption that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies both that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
